justifications.functional_suitability: The architecture covers catalog browsing, multi-currency cart, checkout, recommendations, and shipping integrations. However, dedicated backend handling for customer reviews/ratings (R-03) and electronic book fulfillment workflows are largely omitted beyond frontend widgets.
justifications.performance_efficiency: Targets (1M MAU, <2s load) are thoroughly supported using CloudFront, ElastiCache Redis caching, Aurora Read Replicas, DynamoDB sub-10ms queries, GraphQL payload minimization, and asynchronous processing via Amazon EventBridge and SQS.
justifications.compatibility: The architecture explicitly models third-party shipping APIs (FedEx/DHL) via the Fulfillment Coordinator Component, payment gateways (Stripe/PayPal), identity providers (Auth0/Cognito), and notification systems (SendGrid/Twilio) using REST, HMAC, and standard OpenID Connect protocols.
justifications.usability: Customers (Shoppers) and Store Administrators are well-served with dedicated SPA interfaces and secured API Gateway routes. However, Book Authors/Publishers identified in context diagrams lack dedicated components, portals, or operational endpoints to manage book listings.
justifications.reliability: High availability (99.95% target) and fault tolerance are robustly addressed via ElastiCache Multi-AZ failover, Aurora Global Read Replicas, DynamoDB Global Tables, circuit breakers in Node.js BFF, and SQS Dead-Letter Queues.
justifications.security: OWASP Top-10 mitigations are enforced via AWS WAF and rate limiting, OAuth2/JWT authorizers, internal mTLS via App Mesh, AWS Secrets Manager, and dedicated Consent & Privacy modules ensuring GDPR/CCPA compliance.
justifications.maintainability: Domain services (Checkout, Recommendations, Notification) are decoupled via EventBridge and BFF aggregation. However, centralizing catalog, order, and identity schemas within a single shared Aurora instance creates database coupling across disparate domains.
justifications.portability: Multi-region deployment across the required AWS regions (us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1) is achieved using Aurora Global Databases and DynamoDB Global Tables, although heavy reliance on proprietary AWS services limits cross-provider portability.

PERF-01.justification: CloudFront and S3 serve static assets globally, ElastiCache Redis offloads catalog reads and sessions, while Aurora read replicas handle read-heavy inventory traffic. Horizontal scaling on ECS Fargate ensures backend capacity absorbs 10x traffic spikes.
sensitivity_points: Cache hit ratios on CloudFront and ElastiCache directly dictate backend load
tradeoffs: Aggressive catalog caching increases performance but risks serving slightly stale inventory data

PERF-02.justification: Recommendations compute asynchronously via SageMaker/ECS batch workers and store pre-computed vectors in DynamoDB. The real-time Recommendation API Controller reads pre-computed entries in under 10 ms without placing load on transactional databases.
sensitivity_points: Decoupling batch inference from the online read path isolates customer browsing latency
tradeoffs: Offline batch computation uses fewer runtime resources but yields delayed recommendation updates

AVAIL-01.justification: Order completion emits events to Amazon EventBridge and buffers them in SQS queues with dead-letter capabilities, isolating payment from fulfillment. However, Fulfillment Coordinator is located within the Checkout Service, requiring resilient fallback logic to prevent API timeouts from impacting checkout.
sensitivity_points: Reliability of SQS buffering when third-party fulfillment endpoints become unavailable
tradeoffs: Asynchronous fulfillment improves checkout availability but delays shipping confirmation feedback

AVAIL-02.justification: Aurora Global Databases and DynamoDB Global Tables support cross-region redundancy across us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-1. However, cross-region failover of write traffic requires Aurora replica promotion, and multi-region synchronization for ElastiCache Redis is not explicitly defined.
sensitivity_points: RTO and RPO during cross-region Aurora database failover promotion
tradeoffs: Multi-region data replication enhances regional survivability but adds operational complexity and replication lag

MOD-01.justification: Adding JPY is localized to the SPA Cart & Multi-Currency State Manager and the Checkout Service Cart & Pricing Engine. Third-party integrations like Stripe naturally handle multiple currencies without structural changes across the broader microservice architecture.
sensitivity_points: Centralization of currency and localized pricing rules within dedicated components
tradeoffs: Handling multi-currency conversions centrally simplifies changes but requires consistent downstream exchange rates

MOD-02.justification: Recommendations Service is completely isolated behind GraphQL federation and REST/gRPC interfaces. Swapping algorithms only impacts the Async Batch Inference Worker or Rules & Merchandising Engine without leaking implementation details or requiring changes in upstream containers.
sensitivity_points: Stable interface contracts between Node.js BFF and the Recommendations Service
tradeoffs: Encapsulated algorithmic logic enables rapid iteration at the cost of service-boundary hop latency

SEC-01.justification: Incoming traffic passes through AWS WAF managed rule sets to block SQLi and XSS before hitting internal systems. Parameterized database queries in Spring Boot and PostgreSQL schemas provide secondary layer defenses against injection.
sensitivity_points: Coverage and update cadence of AWS WAF managed inspection rule sets
tradeoffs: Deep packet inspection by WAF adds minor request processing overhead to enhance security

SEC-02.justification: The Consent & Privacy Module, Preference Engine, and Data Access & Privacy Layer explicitly handle GDPR/CCPA purge events via EventBridge/SQS. However, an automated mechanism to purge or anonymize PII in Aurora User Identity and Order schemas is not fully elaborated.
sensitivity_points: Broadcast and verification of purge events across all relational and NoSQL data stores
tradeoffs: Automated cross-service personal data deletion risks accidental data loss if not strictly audited
